items.title: Water is densest at 4 degrees Celsius, not zero
items.claim: Cool any substance and it gets denser as it approaches freezing — except water. Water reaches maximum density at 4 degrees Celsius and then becomes LESS dense as it cools further to 0 degrees Celsius.
items.prompt: Why does ice float on liquid water?

options.text: Trapped air bubbles make ice less dense than liquid water
Hydrogen bonds force water molecules into an open hexagonal lattice on freezing, so solid water occupies about 9 percent more volume than liquid water
Ice is colder, and colder things float
Surface tension on the underside of ice holds it up

items.reveal_title: Hydrogen bonding wins over packing efficiency
items.reveal:
In liquid water, hydrogen bonds break and re-form constantly, and molecules can crowd together. When water freezes, every molecule locks into a tetrahedral arrangement where each oxygen hydrogen-bonds to exactly four neighbours. That structure is open and roomy — about 9 percent more volume than the liquid.

This is why ponds freeze top-down rather than bottom-up. Fish survive winter because the densest water (4 degrees Celsius) sinks and the ice layer insulates everything below. If water behaved normally, lakes would freeze solid and life as we know it could not exist.
items.why: Students assume cooling always increases density. The hydrogen bond's geometry, not the temperature, controls the packing.

items.title: A mole of marshmallows would cover the USA 600 miles deep
items.claim: 6.022 times 10 to the 23 is just a number until you try to picture it. Avogadro's number of marshmallows would bury the entire surface of the United States to a depth of 600 miles.
items.prompt: Roughly how many moles of water molecules are in a single drop (about 0.05 mL)?

options.text: About 0.003 moles, which is roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules
Around 6 times 10 to the 23 — one drop is one mole
About 0.05 moles, the same as the volume in millilitres

items.reveal_title: Even a microscopic drop contains stupefying numbers of molecules
items.reveal:
0.05 mL of water has a mass of 0.05 g. Water is 18 g per mole, so 0.05 / 18 equals about 0.0028 mol. Multiply by Avogadro's number and you get roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules.

If you counted those molecules at one per second, it would take about 50 trillion years — over 3000 times the age of the universe. Chemistry is the study of mind-bending counts of incredibly tiny things.
items.why: The mole is treated as a unit conversion when it should be treated as a stark statement about scale.

items.title: Water dissolves more things than any other liquid
items.claim: Water is called 'the universal solvent'. It dissolves more substances than any other liquid — salts, sugars, gases, many organic molecules. Yet it has only three atoms and a simple structure.
items.prompt: What makes water such a versatile solvent?

options.text: Water is highly polar (large dipole), forms hydrogen bonds with H-bond donors and acceptors, and has a high dielectric constant (around 80) that weakens ionic attractions enough for ions to separate and become solvated
Water is the only liquid on Earth that occurs naturally

items.reveal:
Water's bent shape and large O-H bond polarity give a permanent dipole moment of 1.85 debye. Each water molecule can form up to 4 hydrogen bonds — two as donor, two as acceptor.

Water's dielectric constant of about 80 (vs about 2 for hexane) means it screens ionic charges strongly: a cation and anion that would attract each other electrostatically in vacuum are 80 times less attracted in water, so they separate.

Non-polar substances (oils, wax) lack matching interactions and so won't dissolve. 'Universal' is overstating things — water is just a brilliant solvent for polar and ionic species, and we mostly care about polar and ionic species.
items.why: Water is treated as a passive background. Its chemistry actively shapes whether ions stay dissolved or precipitate.
